questions.q: What kind of market behavior do regime-switching models capture that a single continuous GARCH model cannot?
options: Seasonal patterns within a single year
Gradual, smooth changes in volatility over time
An abrupt, discrete jump between two or more qualitatively different statistical states, rather than a smooth continuous drift
The exact day of the week returns were observed
questions.explain: GARCH captures continuously evolving volatility, but regime-switching models represent markets as alternating between distinct, roughly stable states with their own mean and variance.

questions.q: What defines a Markov chain in the context of Hamilton's Markov-switching model?
options: Regimes change at fixed, predetermined calendar dates
The probability of the next regime depends only on the current regime, not on how long the process has already been in it or anything further in the past
The probability of the next regime depends on the entire history of past regimes
There are always exactly 3 regimes
questions.explain: A Markov chain's defining property is that the next state's probability depends only on the current state (the transition probability matrix p_ij), not on prior history.

questions.q: In the worked example, the fitted mean of the turbulent regime (-0.0022) overshot the true value (-0.0010) and wasn't statistically significant on its own. Why did the model still achieve 97.7% classification accuracy?
options: The model ignored the mean entirely
97.7% accuracy is actually a poor result for this kind of model
The large volatility difference between regimes was easy to detect even though the mean difference was noisy, since the turbulent regime has fewer observations and higher variance
Classification accuracy was actually fabricated
questions.explain: The guide notes that the volatility difference between regimes was large and easy to detect, letting the model classify periods correctly even when the harder-to-pin-down mean was noisy.

questions.q: Why does the guide note that statsmodels doesn't guarantee which fitted regime index corresponds to 'calm' vs. 'turbulent'?
options: Because the model is unreliable and shouldn't be used
Because there are actually 3 regimes, not 2
Because the data was not properly scaled
Because the regime labels (0 or 1) are assigned arbitrarily by the fitting algorithm, so real code needs to identify them after fitting -- e.g., by comparing fitted variances
questions.explain: The fitting procedure doesn't know in advance which index is 'calm' and which is 'turbulent' -- the worked example identifies the turbulent regime as whichever fitted index has the larger sigma^2.

questions.q: In the worked example, how did the fitted transition probabilities compare to the true simulated values?
options: Transition probabilities cannot be estimated from data
Only one transition probability could be estimated
They were wildly different, showing the model failed
p[0->0] was recovered as 0.988 (true 0.970) and p[1->1] as 0.952 (true 0.950) -- both close to their true values
questions.explain: The fitted transition probabilities (0.988 and 0.952) landed close to the true simulated values (0.970 and 0.950), showing the Markov-switching model recovered the regime dynamics well.
